content: Osgood-Schlatter disease, also referred to as tibial tubercle traumatic apophysitis or Louise's knees disease, is a condition characterized by inflammation of the growth plate located at the tibial tuberosity. This condition falls under the category of osteochondritis and is most frequently observed in active boys between the ages of 10 and 15. While it typically affects only one leg, it can occasionally occur in both legs simultaneously. The disease is named after Robert Bayley Osgood, an American surgeon, and Carl Schlatter, a Swiss surgeon, who were the first to describe it. In most cases, the condition resolves on its own over time. The primary cause of Osgood-Schlatter disease is repetitive stress on the patellar tendon, which connects the quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh to the tibia. During an adolescent growth spurt, the tibial tuberosity, which is not yet fully developed, is subjected to stress from the contraction of the quadriceps. This stress can lead to inflammation, avulsion fractures, and subsequent bone growth within the tendon, resulting in the formation of a noticeable lump. Patients with this condition typically present with a visible bump, approximately 2 cm in diameter, at the tibial tubercle. This bump is often painful, particularly during or after high-impact activities, and in some cases, even after less strenuous activities such as climbing stairs. Although the disease is generally benign and self-limiting, symptoms can persist for 2 to 3 years. The condition usually resolves by the end of the growth spurt or, at the latest, when the tibial epiphysis fuses. However, some adults may continue to experience pain when kneeling for the rest of their lives. Analgesic medications can be used to alleviate pain. Physicians often advise patients to temporarily refrain from physical activities that exacerbate the pain until symptoms subside. In cases where symptoms persist, immobilization of the knee with a cast may be necessary. As a last resort, surgical intervention may be considered. This procedure involves drilling multiple holes through the epiphyseal plate under anesthesia to promote fusion and alleviate the condition.
